content:
Some Christian missionaries tell Muslims that their own Quran points them to Jesus (peace be upon him) as the way to heaven. The best-known form of the argument is the "Camel Method", which begins with the Quran's passage on Mary and Jesus in Surah Al ʿImran and moves the reader from there to the New Testament.[1]

The method is real and openly described, and it has been argued over by Christians as fiercely as by Muslims. The question for a Muslim reader is whether the passage it uses says what the method needs it to say.

This article aims to provide context to the method, insha'Allah, in six facts about its history, its use of the Quran, and the debate it provoked. The Quran sets the terms for any such conversation: "come to common terms as between us and you: That we worship none but Allah" (3:64).[2]

Kevin Greeson, a Southern Baptist missionary, set out the method in a training manual published by WIGTake in 2004. Christianity Today reported that it "was detailed in a 2004 book by SBC missionary Kevin Greeson".[3]

Phil Parshall, a veteran missionary to Muslims, reviewed the manual in Evangelical Missions Quarterly in 2005. "A key witness technique," he wrote, "is asking a Muslim to read Surah Al-Imran 3:42-55 from the Quran."[4]

Baptist Press's report on the dispute explains the name. "Every good Muslim knows 99 names for Allah, but there is a 100th name that was revealed only to the camel", the story goes, and the missionary offers to tell what the camel knows.[5]

The same report gives the method's three points. "Using selected verses from the Quran, the method establishes three points: that Isa... is holy, has power over death and knows the way to heaven."[5]

Quran 3:42 to 55 honours Mary and her son. "Allah hath chosen thee and purified thee", the angels tell her (3:42), and they give her "glad tidings of a Word from Him: his name will be Christ Jesus, the son of Mary" (3:45).[2]

Jesus heals the blind and the leper and raises the dead, and each sign is "by Allah's leave" (3:49). He comes as "a messenger to the Children of Israel" (3:49), and God says to him: "I will take thee and raise thee to Myself" (3:55).[2] Every honour in the passage is given by God to a servant.

"The similitude of Jesus before Allah is as that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him: 'Be'. And he was" (3:59).[2] Al-Ṭabarī explains the comparison: God's creation of Jesus without a father is no more wondrous than His creation of Adam without father or mother.[6]

He adds that the verse was revealed as an answer to the Christian delegation from Najran, who argued with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about Jesus.[6] The passage the method uses was itself part of a dialogue with Christians, and it ends with the Quran's conclusion. A reading that stops at verse 55 leaves out the verse that gives the passage its meaning.

In February 2010 Ergun Caner, then president of Liberty Theological Seminary, said of the mission board that used the method: "The IMB is teaching heresy." He called its presentation "absolute, fundamental deception", and added: "You can't start an evangelistic enterprise based on deception."[5]

Roy Oksnevad of the Billy Graham Center at Wheaton called it "sloppy missiology and theology".[3] The International Mission Board's own guidelines of 2007 state that "integrity requires, for example, that we not imply that a false prophet or a body of religious writings other than the Bible are inspired."[5]

Its defenders answered. The board's president, Jerry Rankin, called it "very effective and biblically valid".[3] J. Scott Bridger, a Southern Baptist scholar, has argued at length that Christians may use the Quran as a point of contact, as Arabic-speaking Christians have since the early centuries.[7]

Christianity Today reported "an IMB-sponsored survey in 2002" that counted "some 125,000 Muslims" who had come to faith through the method.[3] The figure comes from the mission board that sponsored the work.

Parshall, who praised the manual, wrote: "I can attest to the credibility of some of the people involved, but not to the veracity of these huge numbers."[4] Nobody outside the missionary networks has published a count.

The bottom line

The Camel Method is an openly evangelical strategy, and its advocates say plainly that the Quran is their starting point and the New Testament their goal. Christian critics called it heresy and deception, its own mission board warned against implying that the Quran is inspired, and its numbers rest on the missionaries' word.

The passage it uses calls Jesus chosen, a Word from God and a worker of signs "by Allah's leave", and four verses later explains his birth by the creation of Adam. Read whole, Surah Al ʿImran leads where Jesus himself leads in the Quran: "worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord" (5:117).[2] We set out the wider case in 5 reasons why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The method and its claims are described in the sources in notes 3 to 5.
  2. Quran 3:42 to 64; 5:116 to 117, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Ken Walker, "Out of Context: Debate over 'Camel Method' Probes Limits of Muslim-Focused Evangelism", Christianity Today, April 2010.
  4. Phil Parshall, review of Kevin Greeson, Camel Training Manual (Midlothian, VA: WIGTake, 2004), Evangelical Missions Quarterly, July 2005.
  5. Bob Allen, "Seminary President Labels Mission Strategy 'Heresy'", Associated Baptist Press, 11 February 2010.
  6. Al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, ed. Maḥmūd Muḥammad Shākir, vol. 6, pp. 468–469, on Quran 3:59.
  7. J. Scott Bridger, Christian Exegesis of the Qurʾān: A Critical Analysis of the Apologetic Use of the Qurʾān in Select Medieval and Contemporary Arabic Texts (Eugene, OR: Pickwick, 2015).
